variations.basis: Varied for this scenario (was 3): the high end of the range given for a year's extension, [1.05, 4.49] m. Gifu Prefectural Research Institute for Agricultural Technology in Hilly and Mountainous Areas, information sheet on raising Vitis coignetiae (yamabudo) from hardwood cuttings (2003), table 2: ten plants from cuttings, planted out in 1990; the longest new shoot of each plant in its first year after planting out was 1.05 to 4.49 m, 3.24 m on average. The range is the shortest and the longest of those ten. The value is taken a little under their mean for a British garden, which is cooler than the mountains of Gifu and where a nursery gives "Up to 2m annually" (https://www.architecturalplants.com/?p=23171). A wall-greening supplier gives "annual shoot growth of 2 - 5 metres" (https://www.fassadengruen.de/en/wild-vines-and-creepers.html). Not measured in Britain.

Varied for this scenario (was 3): the high end of the range given for a year's extension, [1, 3] m. No measurement of a season's extension was found. The RHS has it reach 8 to 12 m in 5 to 10 years (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/747/akebia-quinata/details), which is 0.8 to 2.4 m of height a year with the slow years counted in; an unsourced gardening site gives "2–3 m of new growth a year once established" (https://www.nature-and-garden.com/gardening/akebia-quinata.html). The range is 1 to 3 m from those two, and the value is its top, for a leading stem. Where the plant is invasive, in warmer summers, the GB risk assessment cites "6-12m/yr (Weber, 2003; EPPO, 2021)" (https://www.nonnativespecies.org/assets/Uploads/Akebia-quinata-RA-final_topub-v2.pdf) and itself says that summer temperatures may be too low in Britain. That figure is the plant's mature size in feet turned into metres and may never have been a rate; it is not used.

Varied for this scenario (was 0.6): planted as a nursery specimen standing 3 m, not a young plant

Varied for this scenario (was 1.5): the high end of the range given for a year's extension, [0.47, 1.5] m. Weber (2005), Botanica Helvetica 115: 77-81, abstract: "Current-year shoots were 47-150 cm long", measured at one forest site near Zurich. The range is that; the leading stems are taken to make its top. One shaded site, not a garden. Only the abstract was read: a search excerpt of the full text dates the measuring to the end of May, and if that is right 1.5 m is less than a whole season's growth of the longest shoot. The RHS band (4 to 8 m in 2 to 5 years) is consistent with more.

Varied for this scenario (was 0.8): the high end of the range given for a year's extension, [0.29, 0.97] m. Measured on ivy climbing forest trees in Latvia, at the cold edge of its range: a year's extension of 0.29 to 0.97 m as the mean of each site, and 0.76 m a year over seven years at one of them (Laiviņš, Šnepsts and Treimane 2025, Latvijas Veģetācija 35, read in its English summary and, in translation, its Latvian text; the authors call the data fragmentary). The range is those site means. The value lies inside them, and inside what else is published: a German nursery catalogue's 70 to 100 cm a year from the third year (https://www.lve-baumschule.com/hedera-helix/6353819), and the RHS's sizes, 8 to 12 m in 10 to 20 years (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/43091/hedera-helix/details) and "the height of a two-storey house" in 15 to 20 years (https://www.rhs.org.uk/prevention-protection/ivy-on-buildings). Not measured in Britain, nor on timber.

Varied for this scenario (was [0.2,0.2]): the high end of the range given for the first seasons after planting. The one quantity found, in a nursery catalogue: "initially 10-20 cm a year, from the 3rd to 6th year 70-100 (200) cm". Two slow seasons and then the full rate. The factors are 10, 15 and 20 cm as shares of the 0.8 m this model gives a leading stem: the low end, the value and the high end. Until 14 November 2026 three factors chosen for their shape stood here (0.3, 0.65, 1), a gentler start than the catalogue's. Not measured; no source was found for the gardeners' saying that ivy sleeps, creeps and then leaps.

Varied for this scenario (was 2.1): the high end of the range given for a year's extension, [0.61, 3.05] m. No measurement of a season's extension of wisteria was found in any paper, flora, RHS record or in Bean; the US Forest Service's review says "Rates and distances of spread are not known". The range is the one published statement that gives both ends, Ohio State University's plant record for the genus: "stems during the current season's growth are virtually unbranched, often growing from two to ten feet during the growing season", and "up to ten feet per year under optimum conditions"; in metres. It is said of any stem of the season, in the heat of an American summer, so its low end is low for a leading stem and its high end is a ceiling for a British one. The value is the one figure found for a British garden, at second hand from a nursery's blog: "around seven feet of new growth in one season" (https://blog.thompson-morgan.com/wisteria-masterclass-best-expert-content). Until 14 November 2026 the prototype's 2.6 m stood here. Not measured: the first number to measure on a plant.

Varied for this scenario (was [0.5,0.8]): the high end of the range given for the first seasons after planting. What is published is how long the slow start lasts, not how slow it is: "often slow to establish during its first one to two years of growth, but grows very rapidly thereafter" (Ohio State University, of the genus); "Can be slow to establish" (Missouri Botanical Garden, of this species). The range is that span of time: two slow seasons at its low end, one at its high end, and the value lies between them. The half that a slow season is taken to make is the Wisteria prototype's and has no published counterpart. A trial in Tokyo had large pot-grown Wisteria floribunda reach the end of a 2 m trellis within four months of planting (https://www.tokyo-aff.or.jp/uploaded/attachment/6274.pdf), so a big nursery plant, watered, need not be slow at all.

Ohio State University's plant record for the genus, which names this species: "stems during the current season's growth are virtually unbranched, often growing from two to ten feet during the growing season", and "up to ten feet per year under optimum conditions"; in metres, the range. An arboretum in Kentucky says of this species that it "will grow 10' or more in a single season once established" (https://bcarboretum.org/plants/genus/Wisteria/species/floribunda). The value is the W. sinensis model's, kept so that the two wisterias can be compared: nothing read says by how much this is the less vigorous of the two, and no rate has been measured on it. notes: Hours are direct sun on a clear day in the middle of the month, as the geometry allows: not sunshine records. A half-shaded minute counts as half.
Shares compare a place with an open site at the same spot, so cloud, which falls on both alike, is not in them.
Shade comes from the timber and cables, from what the site declares, and from the leaf other plants carried the season before. A plant is not counted as shading itself.
Warmth, shelter and wind are not light and are not modelled: where a profile asks for a warm or sheltered aspect, nothing here speaks to that.
